main_issue: The guideline text is internally coherent as a standalone vulnerability mechanism (source shape, sink, missing guard, exploit precondition, and safe fix all align around redirect-following SSRF), but the source-reviewed evidence does not establish redirect-following as the shared boundary for any of the cases in this group. The representative_cases list is empty, and the rationale explicitly states that gl_mech_0116 examples mostly establish direct URL/proxy SSRF, renderer external-resource SSRF, or credential/trust-boundary confusion—not redirect-following.

The two cases represent two sub-flavors of renderer-based SSRF (content-triggered external resource resolution in DHIS2/Batik vs. render-service destination SSRF in XWiki/PlantUML), but the core mechanism—rich-content input reaches a renderer/transcoder that initiates network requests without an enforced external-resource policy—is coherent and the boundary text covers both sub-flavors adequately. The missing_guard field already acknowledges renderer-specific variations. Keeping them together as a single mechanism is justified because both are renderer-path SSRF, distinct from direct HTTP proxy or redirect-following SSRF.

The boundary correctly captures the shared source→sink→missing-guard pattern across all four cases. Each case shows attacker-influenced destination material (query param, path info, header, config) flowing into a server-side network client (fetch, RestTemplate, MCP transport, fetcher) without destination validation. The rewrite from redirect-following to direct URL/proxy is justified: redirect following is a guard variant, not the mechanism itself, and the old framing overfits the group name while losing the shared source/sink/guard shape.
